Tool: Google Workspace (Drive, shared drives, Docs, Sheets)
What it is: Cloud storage and real-time co-editing inside the institution's Google account.
Needs served: Store and share files; Collaborate across islands
Pros: Most staff and students already use it. Real-time co-editing. Shared drives belong to the institution, so files survive staff turnover. Forms, Sheets, Looker Studio and Colab sit in the same account.
Cons: A workspace, never a repository: no DOIs, no preservation, and a link dies with its owner's account. Domain restrictions can silently lock out partners on other islands. Native Docs and Sheets files need exporting before anyone else can reuse them.
FAIR note: Working space, not a publication route, so findability, access and reuse are not rated here: a file gets those from the repository it is deposited in. Native Docs and Sheets files exist only inside Google, so export to CSV, ODS or DOCX before depositing.
Fit for small institutions: No extra cost where the institution already licenses it. Keep project files in shared drives, where they stay when people leave.

What it is: Cloud storage, co-editing and meetings inside the institution's Microsoft account.
Needs served: Store and share files; Collaborate across islands
Pros: Full desktop Office compatibility. SharePoint sites and Teams give project spaces with fine-grained permissions. Guest access can let partners on other islands in.
Cons: OneDrive, SharePoint and Teams overlap, and the same file ends up in three places. Permission settings are easy to get wrong. Like any suite, it is working space and cannot publish or preserve.
FAIR note: Working space, not a publication route, so findability, access and reuse are not rated here: a file gets those from the repository it is deposited in. Files are saved as .docx and .xlsx, an ISO standard other software opens, though CSV remains the safer format for data.
Fit for small institutions: Where an institution runs both Google and Microsoft, pick one for research data. Two suites double the places data can hide.

What it is: Open-source file sync and sharing that the institution runs on its own server or through a hosting provider.
Needs served: Store and share files; Collaborate across islands; Handle sensitive data
Pros: Data stays on servers you choose, including servers on the island. No per-user licence. Nextcloud servers at different institutions can share folders with each other.
Cons: Someone has to run it: updates, backups, security patches. For a small IT team that is a permanent load, and a neglected server is worse than a cloud service.
FAIR note: Working space, not a publication route, so findability, access and reuse are not rated here: a file gets those from the repository it is deposited in. Built on open standards (WebDAV), so files move easily.
Fit for small institutions: Worth it only if IT can run a server properly or local data residency is a hard requirement. A managed Nextcloud provider is the middle route.

What it is: Nextcloud-based research storage run by SURF for Dutch research institutions.
Needs served: Store and share files; Collaborate across islands; Handle sensitive data
Pros: Built for research projects: project folders independent of personal accounts, EU data residency, familiar to Dutch partner universities.
Cons: Access runs through a SURF contract. Eligibility for Caribbean institutions: to verify. Check whether a Dutch partner can invite island researchers as external users.
FAIR note: Working space, not a publication route, so findability, access and reuse are not rated here: a file gets those from the repository it is deposited in. Secure, but it cannot publish or preserve.
Fit for small institutions: Most relevant for joint projects with a Dutch university, where the Dutch partner hosts the project folder.

What it is: Simple online forms in Google Workspace, with responses straight into Sheets.
Needs served: Collect survey data
Pros: No training needed. Free with Workspace. Responses land in a Sheet ready for analysis.
Cons: Limited skip logic, no offline collection, no proper codebook. Institutional accounts often default to "Restrict to users in [institution]", which blocks every respondent outside the domain until someone switches it off per form. Not suitable for sensitive data.
FAIR note: Exports CSV, but the questionnaire itself cannot be exported in a standard format for reuse.
Fit for small institutions: Fine for registrations and short surveys. Test every form in a private browser window before sending it off-island.

What it is: Simple online forms in Microsoft 365, with responses into Excel.
Needs served: Collect survey data
Pros: No training needed. Free with Microsoft 365. Results open in Excel.
Cons: Same limits as Google Forms: basic logic, no offline mode, weak for sensitive data. Tenant settings may block external respondents.
FAIR note: CSV and Excel export only.
Fit for small institutions: Fine for registrations and short surveys.

What it is: Free, open-source survey platform from the humanitarian sector, built on ODK, with offline mobile collection.
Needs served: Collect survey data; Collect data offline
Pros: Collects offline on phones and tablets and syncs later. Handles complex logic and several languages in one form. Questionnaires are XLSForm spreadsheets that can be versioned, shared and reused. Exports with labels to SPSS, CSV and Excel.
Cons: The free Community plan has monthly submission and storage limits. Web forms look plain. XLSForm takes a day to learn.
FAIR note: The XLSForm is itself a reusable, documented instrument, which is rare among survey tools.
Fit for small institutions: Strong fit for fieldwork without reliable internet and for zero budgets. Choose the EU or global server deliberately: it decides where the data sits.

What it is: Open-source survey software, free to self-host or paid as a cloud service.
Needs served: Collect survey data; Handle sensitive data
Pros: Powerful branching and quotas. One instrument can carry English, Dutch, Papiamento and Spanish versions. Self-hosting keeps responses on the institution's own server.
Cons: Self-hosting needs IT capacity; the cloud version is paid. Interface feels dated. No offline mode in the standard setup.
FAIR note: Exports the survey structure (.lss) and the data to CSV, SPSS and R.
Fit for small institutions: A good institutional survey server if IT can host it. One well-run server could serve partners on other islands too.

What it is: Commercial enterprise survey platform, common at universities abroad.
Needs served: Collect survey data
Pros: Capable logic, quotas, panels and reporting. Many visiting researchers and partner universities already use it.
Cons: Expensive institutional licences and lock-in: surveys and data live on the vendor's platform. Hard to justify for a small institution when free tools cover most needs.
FAIR note: Exports data to CSV and SPSS; the survey file (.qsf) only opens in Qualtrics.
Fit for small institutions: Often reachable through a partner university's licence on a joint project, which avoids buying it locally.

What it is: Data capture system built for clinical and health research; free licence for non-profits in the REDCap consortium, but the institution must host it.
Needs served: Collect survey data; Collect data offline; Handle sensitive data
Pros: Designed for sensitive data: audit trails, user roles, de-identified exports, longitudinal designs. Offline mobile app.
Cons: Needs an institution to host and administer it under a consortium licence. Overkill outside health and longitudinal studies.
FAIR note: Exports to CSV, SPSS, Stata and R with a data dictionary that documents the instrument.
Fit for small institutions: Ask a partner university or hospital that already runs REDCap about access before considering a local install.

What it is: General-purpose open repository run by CERN. Every upload gets a DOI.
Needs served: Publish a dataset; Mint DOIs; Archive long term; Publish teaching materials; Publish reports and theses
Pros: Free DOIs for anything: data, reports, slides, code, lessons. Versioning keeps one DOI for the latest version and one per version. Communities give an institution or network its own collection at no cost. GitHub integration archives each code release automatically. Up to 50 GB per record.
Cons: Light curation: nobody checks data quality or documentation, so FAIR quality rests on the depositor. Generic metadata. Restricted access exists but is basic, so keep sensitive personal data out. Grant metadata is checked against OpenAIRE, which rejected the DCDC NWO project code in May 2026.
FAIR note: Findable and accessible by design. Interoperability depends on the file formats uploaded. A licence is required at deposit.
Fit for small institutions: The quickest route to DOIs for an institution without its own repository. A community works as the institution's shop window. The DCDC-Network community already exists and partners can submit to it.

What it is: Free project workspace from the Center for Open Science that can be made public with DOIs, plus preregistrations and preprints.
Needs served: Publish a dataset; Mint DOIs; Collaborate across islands; Publish teaching materials
Pros: One place for the whole project, private while working and public at the end. Preregistration built in. Connects to Google Drive, GitHub and Dropbox. Storage region can be set to the EU. Good for teaching open science practice step by step.
Cons: Storage caps per project, lower for private than public projects. Thinner metadata than Zenodo or Dataverse. Not designed for sensitive personal data.
FAIR note: DOIs for public projects and registrations. FAIR quality rests on how well the project is documented.
Fit for small institutions: Fits teams that want to work openly from day one, and methods courses in teacher training.

What it is: Commercial repository with a free public site and a paid institutional version.
Needs served: Publish a dataset; Mint DOIs; Run own repository
Pros: Polished interface with in-browser previews of many file types. The institutional version gives a branded repository with DOIs without running any servers.
Cons: Free accounts have storage limits. The institutional version is an annual contract with a commercial company (Digital Science).
FAIR note: DOIs and licences on every item; standard metadata harvesting.
Fit for small institutions: Figshare for Institutions is the own-repository-without-own-IT option, if budget exists.

What it is: Free Dataverse repository open to researchers worldwide, strong for tabular social science data.
Needs served: Publish a dataset; Mint DOIs; Archive long term
Pros: Converts SPSS, Stata and R files into archival formats and extracts variable-level metadata. Restricted files with access requests and guestbooks. An institution can create its own branded collection inside it. Same software as DataverseNL, so skills transfer.
Cons: Per-researcher storage and file-size limits. US-hosted. Busier interface than Zenodo. Not for highly sensitive data.
FAIR note: Among the strongest on interoperability, thanks to file conversion and variable-level metadata.
Fit for small institutions: A strong choice for survey data, especially when some files need restricted access.

What it is: Dataverse service hosted by DANS for participating Dutch institutions, each managing its own collection.
Needs served: Publish a dataset; Mint DOIs; Run own repository
Pros: Same software as Harvard Dataverse, hosted in the Netherlands, with the institution in control of its own collection and curation.
Cons: Requires an institutional agreement and a local administrator. Eligibility and current terms for Caribbean institutions: to verify.
FAIR note: As Harvard Dataverse.
Fit for small institutions: Only relevant if an institution wants its own curated collection and qualifies.

What it is: The Dutch national centre of expertise and repository for research data (KNAW and NWO), with a Data Station for social sciences and humanities.
Needs served: Publish a dataset; Mint DOIs; Archive long term; Handle sensitive data
Pros: Certified long-term archive with expert curation. NWO's own data institute, so a natural home for NWO-funded data. Supports restricted access under conditions the depositor sets.
Cons: Deposit terms and costs for depositors at Caribbean institutions: to verify. Curation takes time and asks for good documentation up front.
FAIR note: Curation raises FAIR quality instead of leaving it to the depositor.
Fit for small institutions: Ask DANS once on behalf of the network; one answer serves all four institutions.

What it is: Repository of the Dutch technical universities for science, engineering and design data.
Needs served: Publish a dataset; Mint DOIs; Archive long term
Pros: Certified long-term archive with curation, strong for technical, environmental and sensor data.
Cons: Oriented to engineering and natural sciences. Terms for depositors outside the member universities: to verify.
FAIR note: Curated, certified repository.
Fit for small institutions: Relevant for environmental and marine monitoring data.

What it is: Specialist repository at Syracuse University for qualitative and multi-method social science data.
Needs served: Publish a dataset; Mint DOIs; Handle sensitive data; Archive long term
Pros: Curators help with consent, de-identification and access controls, the hardest part of sharing interviews and field notes. Understands qualitative data instead of treating it as a pile of files.
Cons: Institutional membership model; check deposit terms for non-members. US-based.
FAIR note: Built for the case generic repositories handle badly: qualitative data that can only be shared under conditions.
Fit for small institutions: Worth knowing before a qualitative project starts, because the consent form has to allow the sharing.

What it is: Cooperative digital library of Caribbean partner institutions for heritage collections, newspapers, reports and theses.
Needs served: Archive long term; Publish reports and theses
Pros: Regional visibility and a Caribbean readership. Partner model suited to institutions with small collections. Good for grey literature that otherwise disappears.
Cons: For documents and heritage material; research datasets belong elsewhere. Partner arrangements to check with the library.
FAIR note: Open access and well indexed in the region; check how identifiers and licences are recorded.
Fit for small institutions: A natural home for theses and institutional reports. Ask whether the library is already a partner.

What it is: The open-source repository platform behind Zenodo, for institutions that want to run their own.
Needs served: Run own repository; Mint DOIs; Publish a dataset
Pros: Modern, standards-based repository with the Zenodo feature set under the institution's own name. DOIs through the institution's DataCite prefix.
Cons: Needs developers and system administrators to install, run and upgrade. Far too heavy for one small IT team.
FAIR note: Designed for FAIR from the ground up.
Fit for small institutions: Sensible only as a shared service, for example one Dutch Caribbean repository serving all islands. That answers the survey's wish for a Caribbean repository, and it is a multi-year commitment.

What it is: Widely used open-source institutional repository software for publications, theses and reports.
Needs served: Run own repository; Publish reports and theses; Archive long term
Pros: Mature and used by thousands of universities. Harvested by Google Scholar and aggregators through OAI-PMH. Hosted versions remove the need for a local server.
Cons: Self-hosting needs IT; hosted versions cost money. Stronger for documents than for datasets.
FAIR note: Standard metadata harvesting. DOIs need a DataCite or Crossref membership.
Fit for small institutions: The classic choice for theses and reports. Compare it with a free Zenodo community first.

What it is: Gives the institution its own DOI prefix to mint DOIs for anything it hosts: datasets, reports, theses, lessons.
Needs served: Mint DOIs; Run own repository
Pros: Own prefix and full control. The Fabrica web tool lets staff mint DOIs by hand, no software needed. Joining through a consortium costs less than direct membership.
Cons: Annual fee. A DOI is a promise: the institution must keep every landing page alive and the metadata current, indefinitely.
FAIR note: DOIs are the core of Findable. DataCite metadata is harvested by every major discovery service.
Fit for small institutions: Only needed when the institution hosts outputs itself. Zenodo, Dataverse, OSF and Figshare give DOIs free under their own prefix.

What it is: DOIs and citation linking for journal articles, books, proceedings and report series.
Needs served: Mint DOIs; Publish reports and theses
Pros: The standard for journals: DOIs, reference linking and citation counts. Most indexes require it. Small publishers can join through a sponsor.
Cons: Annual fee plus a fee per DOI. Someone has to deposit proper metadata for every item.
FAIR note: Rich citation metadata.
Fit for small institutions: Relevant only for an institution that publishes a journal or a formal series.

What it is: Free persistent identifier for each researcher, linking them to their outputs across systems.
Needs served: Identify people and organisations
Pros: Free for individuals and takes five minutes. Funders increasingly ask for it. Repositories such as Zenodo fill it in automatically.
Cons: Only as good as researchers keep it. Institutional membership, needed to push affiliations into records, costs money.
FAIR note: Disambiguates people across every system that uses it.
Fit for small institutions: Ask every researcher and thesis supervisor to register now; membership can wait.

What it is: Free, open identifier for research organisations, used in DOI and ORCID metadata.
Needs served: Identify people and organisations
Pros: Free. Makes the institution recognisable in repository and funder metadata, so outputs are counted to it. Zenodo, DataCite and ORCID all use it.
Cons: Nothing beyond keeping the record current when names or websites change.
FAIR note: The organisation-level counterpart to ORCID. Crediting the organisation supports provenance.
Fit for small institutions: Checked 10 Sep 2026: UA (ror.org/05cdyhf91) and UoC (ror.org/02a46nr93) have ROR IDs; no record found for USM or IPA. Requesting one is free, through a form on ror.org.

What it is: Menu-driven statistics package, long the default in social science and education.
Needs served: Statistical analysis; Teach data analysis
Pros: Most staff trained in social science already know it. Menus lower the barrier for occasional users. Clean output tables. Syntax exists for those who use it.
Cons: A recurring licence cost that small institutions feel, with modules priced separately. Point-and-click work cannot be reproduced unless people save syntax, and most do not. Skills carry over poorly to data science.
FAIR note: .sav files open in R, Python, Stata, jamovi and PSPP, so the data is not locked in. Saved syntax makes the analysis repeatable, though rerunning it needs a licence. Deposit CSV plus a codebook.
Fit for small institutions: DCDC survey respondents asked for free alternatives to paid licences. PSPP, jamovi and JASP cover most teaching needs, and the R for SPSS Users course is the bridge to R.

What it is: Free replacement for SPSS from the GNU project, with similar menus and syntax.
Needs served: Statistical analysis; Teach data analysis
Pros: Free. Looks and works like SPSS, reads .sav files and runs much SPSS syntax. No licence administration at all.
Cons: Covers little beyond classical statistics. Slower development and a smaller community.
FAIR note: Open formats; syntax files make work reproducible.
Fit for small institutions: A drop-in for introductory statistics teaching on a zero budget.

What it is: Free, open-source statistics package built on R, with a spreadsheet-style interface.
Needs served: Statistical analysis; Teach data analysis; Reproducible analysis
Pros: The friendliest free alternative to SPSS for teaching. Results update live when data changes. Can show the R code behind each analysis, which makes it a bridge to R. Opens .sav and .csv. Modules add methods.
Cons: Weak at heavy data management and large datasets. Module quality varies.
FAIR note: Open file formats; syntax mode supports reproducibility.
Fit for small institutions: A strong default for teacher training and first-year statistics.

What it is: Free, open-source statistics package from the University of Amsterdam, classical and Bayesian.
Needs served: Statistical analysis; Teach data analysis
Pros: Clean interface and APA-formatted output that students can paste into a thesis. Bayesian methods alongside classical ones. Rich teaching material.
Cons: Limited data cleaning and transformation; data needs preparing elsewhere first.
FAIR note: Open formats; analyses are saved with the data in one .jasp file.
Fit for small institutions: Pairs with jamovi for teaching. Choose one per course.

What it is: Free statistical programming language, used with the RStudio editor from Posit. The network's teaching language.
Needs served: Statistical analysis; Econometrics and time series; Reproducible analysis; Machine learning; Dashboards and visualisation; Teach data analysis
Pros: Free, with no licence to renew. Every step lives in a script, so analyses can be rerun and checked. Thousands of packages, including haven for SPSS and Stata files and Quarto for reports. Strong community: the Carpentries, R-Ladies, LatinR.
Cons: Steeper start than menu-driven packages; the first weeks need structured support. Installing R and packages on locked-down institutional laptops needs IT help.
FAIR note: Scripts plus open formats make R one of the strongest tools for reproducible, reusable analysis.
Fit for small institutions: DCDC already teaches it: R for SPSS Users (Aruba, April 2026) and Blue Wave (Curaçao, September 2026). Agree admin rights or a lab image with IT before a course starts.

What it is: RStudio in the browser, with a free tier and paid plans for teaching.
Needs served: Teach data analysis; Reproducible analysis
Pros: Nothing to install: every student gets the same working setup in a browser on any laptop. The instructor can hand out a prepared project.
Cons: The free tier limits hours and projects, so a full class needs a paid plan. Data sits on a US cloud; keep sensitive data off it.
FAIR note: As R.
Fit for small institutions: The fallback when installation would eat the first morning of a workshop.

What it is: Free general-purpose programming language with a large data stack: pandas, statsmodels, scikit-learn, Jupyter.
Needs served: Statistical analysis; Machine learning; Reproducible analysis; Dashboards and visualisation; Teach data analysis
Pros: One language for analysis, web scraping, automation and machine learning. A widely demanded skill on the job market. Jupyter notebooks mix code, output and text.
Cons: Statistical output is less report-ready for social science than R or Stata. Managing package versions confuses beginners. Check Anaconda's licence terms before installing it institution-wide; Miniforge (conda-forge) avoids the question.
FAIR note: As R.
Fit for small institutions: Choose per programme: R leans to statistics and social science, Python to data science and engineering.

What it is: Jupyter notebooks for Python in the browser, tied to a Google account.
Needs served: Machine learning; Teach data analysis; Reproducible analysis
Pros: Nothing to install. Works with Google Drive, so it fits institutions on Google Workspace. Free GPU time for machine learning exercises.
Cons: Sessions time out and unsaved work disappears. Workspace administrators can switch it off for institutional accounts. Data goes to Google.
FAIR note: Notebooks are open .ipynb files; reproducibility needs package versions recorded.
Fit for small institutions: Ask IT whether it is enabled on institutional accounts before planning a course around it.

What it is: Commercial statistics package, standard in economics, epidemiology and survey research.
Needs served: Statistical analysis; Econometrics and time series; Reproducible analysis
Pros: Consistent command language and excellent documentation. Do-files make reproducible work a habit. Strong on panel data, survey weights and microeconometrics. The working language of many economics departments and journals.
Cons: Licence per user, perpetual or annual, and cheaper editions limit dataset size. Closed source.
FAIR note: .dta files open in R and Python, and do-files document the full analysis, though rerunning it needs a Stata licence.
Fit for small institutions: Worth it where staff publish in economics or health. R covers the same ground for free.

What it is: Commercial package for time-series econometrics and forecasting, widely used at central banks and finance ministries.
Needs served: Econometrics and time series
Pros: Fast route to time-series models, forecasts and macro models without much coding. A shared language with central bank and ministry economists, which matters for policy work.
Cons: Windows only and expensive. Workfiles (.wf1) are awkward to open without EViews. Many users work by menu, so results are hard to reproduce unless they write programs.
FAIR note: Export series to CSV for any deposit. Save programs; menu history is lost.
Fit for small institutions: For teaching econometrics, gretl covers most of the ground for free. Keep EViews where graduates will work alongside central banks.

What it is: Free, open-source econometrics package with menus and scripting.
Needs served: Econometrics and time series; Statistical analysis; Teach data analysis
Pros: Covers most of what EViews and Stata do in an econometrics course, at no cost. Opens Stata, SPSS and EViews files. Datasets from standard textbooks (Wooldridge, Stock and Watson and others) are available inside it.
Cons: Smaller user base and little used in the policy world, so graduates still meet EViews or Stata at work. Fewer cutting-edge methods.
FAIR note: Scripts and open formats.
Fit for small institutions: Replaces licence spending in econometrics teaching.

What it is: The universal starting point for data entry and quick tables.
Needs served: Statistical analysis; Dashboards and visualisation
Pros: Everyone has one and knows the basics. Fine for data entry, small tables and quick charts.
Cons: Silent errors: automatic conversion of dates, codes and leading zeros. No record of the steps taken, so analyses cannot be checked or repeated. Merged cells and colour-coding make data unreadable to other software.
FAIR note: Save as CSV with a separate codebook for reuse.
Fit for small institutions: Teach data organisation in spreadsheets (Broman and Woo 2018) before any other tool. It prevents most cleaning problems later.

What it is: Commercial qualitative analysis software from Lumivero, the best known in universities.
Needs served: Qualitative coding; Mixed methods
Pros: Handles large projects with text, audio, video, surveys and social media. Extensive training material and a big user base. Team version for shared projects.
Cons: Expensive subscription. Windows and Mac versions differ. Steep for occasional users. Projects live in a proprietary format.
FAIR note: Supports the REFI-QDA exchange standard, so projects can move to other tools, though not always completely.
Fit for small institutions: Hard to justify on a small budget unless a research group uses it heavily.

What it is: Commercial qualitative analysis software with desktop and web versions.
Needs served: Qualitative coding; Mixed methods; Collaborate across islands
Pros: The web version lets a team code together from different islands. Strong network views of codes. Affordable student licences. AI-assisted coding.
Cons: Subscription cost. The AI features send data to external services, which consent forms and ethics approval may not cover.
FAIR note: Supports REFI-QDA export.
Fit for small institutions: A good fit where teams at different institutions code the same material.

What it is: Commercial qualitative and mixed-methods software.
Needs served: Qualitative coding; Mixed methods
Pros: Identical on Windows and Mac. Strong on mixed methods: links codes to survey variables, with a statistics module. Clear interface. A free Reader lets others open projects.
Cons: Paid, with a large gap between student and staff prices. AI features raise the same consent questions as ATLAS.ti.
FAIR note: Supports REFI-QDA export.
Fit for small institutions: Suits institutions doing mixed-methods evaluation, such as education research.

What it is: Web-based qualitative and mixed-methods tool, paid per user per month.
Needs served: Qualitative coding; Mixed methods; Collaborate across islands
Pros: Pay only for the months in use, which suits short projects and thesis students. Browser-based teamwork. Low barrier to start.
Cons: Data sits on the vendor's US cloud. Monthly costs add up over a long project. Limited export options, and it needs a steady internet connection.
FAIR note: Limited exports make it the hardest of these to move away from.
Fit for small institutions: Good for a single short project; a poor home for an institution's long-term qualitative material.

What it is: Free, open-source tool for highlighting and tagging documents, in the browser or on the desktop.
Needs served: Qualitative coding; Teach data analysis
Pros: Learnable in an hour. Free, with a public server to try it and the option to host your own for team projects. Ideal for teaching the logic of coding before anyone buys anything.
Cons: Text only: no audio, video or images. No advanced queries or visualisations.
FAIR note: Exports codebooks and highlights in open formats, including a REFI-QDA codebook.
Fit for small institutions: A strong starting point for teaching qualitative analysis in teacher training.

What it is: Free, open-source desktop tool for coding text, images, audio and video.
Needs served: Qualitative coding
Pros: Surprisingly complete for free software: codes text, images, audio and video, with reports and case attributes. Imports and exports REFI-QDA projects, so work can move to and from NVivo, ATLAS.ti and MAXQDA.
Cons: Single-user desktop tool. Maintained by a small team. Less polished than the commercial tools.
FAIR note: Strong on interoperability through full REFI-QDA project support.
Fit for small institutions: The free option once Taguette becomes too limited.

What it is: Free, reduced version of Provalis QDA Miner for Windows.
Needs served: Qualitative coding
Pros: Free and simple for basic coding and retrieval.
Cons: Windows only. Limited features; the full version is paid.
FAIR note: Few export options.
Fit for small institutions: Mostly overtaken by Taguette and QualCoder for zero-budget use.

What it is: Free, open-source transcription that runs entirely on the user's own computer, based on the Whisper speech model.
Needs served: Transcribe interviews; Handle sensitive data
Pros: Audio never leaves the computer, which settles the privacy question that cloud transcription raises. Identifies speakers. Output opens in an editor for correction.
Cons: Slow on ordinary laptops without a good graphics card. Papiamento is not among Whisper's listed languages, so Papiamento interviews need testing before anyone relies on it.
FAIR note: Plain-text and standard subtitle outputs.
Fit for small institutions: Test with one real Papiamento recording before recommending it to students.

Tool: Cloud transcription services (for example Otter.ai, Microsoft 365 transcription)
What it is: Automatic transcription run on a vendor's servers.
Needs served: Transcribe interviews
Pros: Fast and convenient, with good accuracy for English.
Cons: Recordings are uploaded to the vendor, and some terms allow use for model training. Consent forms rarely cover this. Papiamento and code-switching untested.
FAIR note: Exports text; the audio is out of the researcher's control once uploaded.
Fit for small institutions: Check what the consent form promised participants before uploading anything.

What it is: Free, open-source visual programming tool for machine learning and data visualisation, from the University of Ljubljana.
Needs served: Machine learning; Dashboards and visualisation; Teach data analysis
Pros: Drag-and-drop workflows make machine learning teachable without code. Excellent teaching material, with add-ons for text mining.
Cons: Hits a ceiling on large data and custom methods. Workflows are harder to hand over than scripts.
FAIR note: Workflows are saved as files that record every step, and the data stays in open formats.
Fit for small institutions: A good first taste of data science for students and staff who will not code.

What it is: Free, open-source desktop tool for building data workflows visually, with paid server products.
Needs served: Machine learning; Reproducible analysis; Dashboards and visualisation
Pros: Visual workflows record every cleaning and analysis step, which makes them repeatable. Strong at combining data from many sources. Common in business analytics.
Cons: Heavy installation. Large workflows get visually cluttered. Collaboration and scheduling need paid products.
FAIR note: Workflows record the whole process: reproducibility for people who do not code.
Fit for small institutions: Suits analysts in government and business who repeat the same data preparation every month.

What it is: Free dashboard tool from Google, connected to Sheets and other sources.
Needs served: Dashboards and visualisation
Pros: Free and already inside the Google account. Dashboards update from a Sheet and share like a Google Doc.
Cons: Limited data modelling. Dashboards break when the underlying Sheet changes. Nothing is archived, so there is no persistent record.
FAIR note: A communication layer, not an archive. Findability and access come from where the data itself is deposited.
Fit for small institutions: Quick wins for communicating institutional figures.

What it is: Microsoft's business intelligence and dashboard tool.
Needs served: Dashboards and visualisation
Pros: Strong data modelling. Common in government and business, so it is a marketable skill. Fits Microsoft 365 institutions.
Cons: The desktop app is Windows only. Sharing dashboards needs paid licences. "Publish to web" makes the data visible to anyone, a known cause of accidental leaks.
FAIR note: A communication layer, not an archive. Findability and access come from where the data itself is deposited.
Fit for small institutions: A useful skill for graduates heading into government.

What it is: Commercial visual analytics tool; Tableau Public is free but publishes everything openly.
Needs served: Dashboards and visualisation
Pros: Polished, fast visual exploration. Free licences for teachers and students through Tableau's academic programme. Tableau Public doubles as a free student portfolio.
Cons: Commercial licences are expensive. On Tableau Public every workbook and its data are public.
FAIR note: A communication layer, not an archive. Findability and access come from where the data itself is deposited.
Fit for small institutions: Academic licences make it free for teaching; check eligibility per institution.

What it is: Code-based dashboards and reports built in R or Python, free and open source.
Needs served: Dashboards and visualisation; Reproducible analysis
Pros: Fully reproducible: the dashboard is code anyone can rerun. Static Quarto dashboards can be hosted free on GitHub Pages.
Cons: Requires R or Python skills. Interactive Shiny apps need a server to run on.
FAIR note: Dashboard, data and code can be deposited together under one DOI, and the repository supplies findability and access.
Fit for small institutions: The natural next step for R course graduates.

What it is: Hosting for code and documents under version control (git), with free websites through GitHub Pages.
Needs served: Version control; Publish teaching materials; Collaborate across islands
Pros: The standard place to share code. Free organisation accounts, and free GitHub Education benefits for teachers and students. Linked to Zenodo, each release can receive a DOI automatically; the DCDC R course got its DOI this way. Pages turns a repository into a website.
Cons: Git has a real learning curve. Owned by Microsoft. Repositories can be deleted, so archive releases in Zenodo.
FAIR note: With Zenodo archiving, every release is findable and citable.
Fit for small institutions: An institutional organisation keeps repositories with the institution when people leave. Decide who administers it and how new repositories are announced.

What it is: Code hosting with version control, as a service or self-hosted.
Needs served: Version control
Pros: Can be self-hosted, so code stays on the institution's servers. Built-in automation (CI).
Cons: Self-hosting needs IT. Smaller academic community than GitHub, and no automatic Zenodo archiving.
FAIR note: Open formats throughout; archive releases by hand.
Fit for small institutions: Only if code must stay on local servers.

What it is: Code hosting with version control (git), run by a non-profit on the open-source Forgejo software, with free websites through Codeberg Pages.
Needs served: Version control; Publish teaching materials; Collaborate across islands
Pros: No company behind it: Codeberg e.V., a non-profit association in Germany, runs it on donations, with servers in the EU. Works like GitHub, so the same git skills carry over. Raised at the Carpentries instructor training (October 2026) as an open alternative to GitHub.
Cons: Meant for free and open-source work, so not a home for private institutional repositories. Smaller community than GitHub, and no automatic Zenodo archiving, so a release gets its DOI only when deposited by hand.
FAIR note: Open formats throughout; archive releases in Zenodo by hand for a DOI.
Fit for small institutions: A good home for open teaching material and public code with no licence or vendor tie. Keep a GitHub or GitLab organisation where private repositories are needed.

What it is: Open-source system for writing reports, websites, books and slides that contain R or Python code and output.
Needs served: Reproducible analysis; Publish teaching materials; Publish reports and theses
Pros: One source file produces HTML, PDF and Word. Figures and numbers regenerate from the data, so reports stay correct when the data changes.
Cons: Requires comfort with plain-text writing (Markdown) and some code.
FAIR note: Plain-text sources and open outputs.
Fit for small institutions: Useful for recurring reports rebuilt every quarter or year.

What it is: Framework for building open lessons as websites, used by the Carpentries.
Needs served: Publish teaching materials
Pros: Lessons become open websites that others can copy and adapt. Access to the Carpentries community for review. Both DCDC courses are built on it.
Cons: Needs GitHub and R set up. The format suits workshops better than semester courses.
FAIR note: Lessons are plain-text sources with open outputs. Releases archived through Zenodo get their DOI there.
Fit for small institutions: Lets one institution adapt another island's lesson instead of starting again.

What it is: Web tool for writing data management plans against funder templates, run by the UK Digital Curation Centre.
Needs served: Data management planning
Pros: Funder templates with guidance. Plans can be shared with co-authors and reviewers. Free for individual researchers.
Cons: Institutional customisation and reporting are paid. Check that the template you need, NWO's for example, is listed.
FAIR note: A good plan is where FAIR starts: it fixes formats, licences and repository before the data exists.
Fit for small institutions: Useful straight away for grant applications, with no institutional subscription needed to start.

Tool: Microsoft Copilot Chat (with a work or school account)
What it is: AI chat signed in with the institution's Microsoft 365 account (called Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat until 2026). Prompts and uploaded files leave the device but stay under the institution's Microsoft agreement.
Needs served: Use AI tools safely
Runs on: Web, Windows, Mac, mobile, inside Outlook and Teams
Pros: No extra licence cost on Microsoft 365 A1, A3 and A5 education plans. Prompts are not used to train Microsoft's models and are processed under the institution's data processing agreement. Retention follows the institution's own Microsoft 365 policies. The obvious first step for an institution that already runs Outlook and Office.
Cons: Students need to be 13 or older and an administrator has to switch it on for them. Web searches it runs go to Bing under consumer terms, which an administrator can switch off. Outside the EU the processing can be routed to other regions. The free version only sees files a user uploads; the paid Microsoft Copilot licence adds the institution's own files and mail.
FAIR note: Outputs cannot be reproduced exactly, because the model changes without notice. Record the prompt and date when an output feeds into research.
Fit for small institutions: Check whether IT has already enabled it before anyone pays for a separate AI account. A sanctioned option also moves work off personal accounts.

Tool: Gemini app and Gemini Notebook (Google Workspace for Education)
What it is: AI chat and a source-grounded notebook (formerly NotebookLM) signed in with the institution's Google account. Data leaves the device but stays under the Workspace for Education terms.
Needs served: Use AI tools safely
Pros: Included in every Workspace for Education edition at no charge. Google states the data is not reviewed by people or used to train its models. Gemini Notebook answers from the sources a user uploads, which suits reading and summarising a set of documents.
Cons: Paid Gemini add-ons need users designated 18 or older. Under-18 users get a restricted version. Only covers people with an institutional Google account, so partners at other institutions are outside it.
FAIR note: As for any hosted model: keep the prompt, sources and date with any output used in research.
Fit for small institutions: The first step for institutions on Google Workspace. An administrator has to confirm it is switched on.

Tool: ChatGPT Edu and Claude for Education
What it is: Institution-wide workspaces from OpenAI and Anthropic, bought by the university for staff and students.
Needs served: Use AI tools safely
Pros: Content is not used for training by default. Accounts belong to the institution, so access ends when someone leaves. Admin controls over who uses what.
Cons: Prices are not published and are negotiated per institution. A recurring per-user cost on top of licences the institution may already hold.
FAIR note: As for any hosted model.
Fit for small institutions: Only worth considering once the AI included in the existing Microsoft or Google licence has been tried and found short.

Tool: Personal AI accounts (free or paid ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini)
What it is: An AI account a person signs up for privately, outside any agreement with the institution.
Needs served: Use AI tools safely
Pros: Easy to start, and many staff and students already use one. Personal paid plans give access to the strongest models.
Cons: The terms are between the person and the vendor. ChatGPT's personal plans use conversations for training unless the user switches it off. Claude's personal plans let the user choose, with conversations kept 5 years if training is on and 30 days if it is off. The institution has no say over any of it.
FAIR note: As for any hosted model.
Fit for small institutions: Public information only. Without a sanctioned alternative, this is where institutional data ends up.

Tool: Claude Code and other AI coding agents
What it is: An assistant that runs in a terminal on the user's own computer, reads and edits files, and runs code. The model itself runs on the vendor's servers.
Needs served: Use AI tools safely; Reproducible analysis
Pros: Works directly on scripts and documents, so analysis and reporting can be scripted and rerun. Strong for R and Python work.
Cons: Runs locally but sends prompts and every file it reads to the vendor. Logged in with a personal Pro or Max account, the personal terms above apply. Under a Team, Enterprise or API account, data is not used for training and is deleted within 30 days; zero retention is available case by case for qualifying enterprise accounts. Keep confidential folders out of the folder it works in.
FAIR note: The scripts it writes are reproducible. Its own suggestions are not, so the script is the record, not the conversation.
Fit for small institutions: For staff who already script their analysis. Use it under an institutional or API account for anything beyond public data.

What it is: Desktop app that downloads open AI models and runs them entirely on the user's own computer.
Needs served: Use AI tools safely; Handle sensitive data
Pros: Nothing typed into it leaves the device; internet is only needed to download the app and models. No account, no agreement, no recurring cost. Suits confidential material such as interview transcripts or student records.
Cons: Local models are weaker than the hosted ones. Needs a reasonably recent laptop: about 16 GB of memory for the common 7 to 8 billion parameter models. Free for use at work, but not open source.
FAIR note: A fixed model version on a local machine behaves the same over time, unlike a hosted model.
Fit for small institutions: The answer when the data may not leave the institution at all.

What it is: Open-source tool that runs AI models on the user's own computer, from the command line or behind other apps.
Needs served: Use AI tools safely; Handle sensitive data
Pros: Local models stay on the machine. MIT licence. Widely supported by other tools, including R and Python packages.
Cons: Since 2025 it also offers cloud models, marked with a cloud tag, which run on Ollama's servers. Staff need to know which kind they are running. Same hardware needs as LM Studio.
FAIR note: As for LM Studio, provided the model is a local one.
Fit for small institutions: For IT staff or analysts setting up a local model others can use.

Tool: AI-writing detectors (for example Turnitin's AI indicator)
What it is: Tools that estimate whether a text was written by AI.
Needs served: Set AI rules for teaching
Pros: Can prompt a conversation with a student about how a text was made.
Cons: Unreliable as evidence. One study found detectors flagged 61 percent of essays by non-native English writers as AI-written, against very few by native writers (Liang et al., Patterns, 2023). OpenAI withdrew its own detector in July 2023 for low accuracy. In multilingual classrooms the false positives land on the students least able to contest them.
FAIR note: Not a data tool.
Fit for small institutions: Never the sole basis for an academic integrity decision. Assessment design, such as oral follow-up and drafts handed in along the way, does more.
